title: Black Sea Incidents Surge Tenfold, Raising Risk NATO Is Drawn Into War
excerpt: Drones, mines and ship attacks in the Black Sea have risen from fewer than 50 incidents in 2025 to as many as 500 this year, NATO's spokesperson told CBS News, on a sea bordered by three alliance members.
body:
• Incidents involving drones, mines and commercial ships in the Black Sea have risen from fewer than 50 in 2025 to between 400 and 500 this year, according to NATO military spokesperson Colonel Martin O'Donnell.
  • At least 40 sailors have been killed in the Black Sea this year, more than the 25 killed in the Strait of Hormuz in the same period, according to maritime bodies cited by CBS News.
  • Three of the six countries bordering the Black Sea — Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey — are NATO members, so a strike in their waters could trigger the alliance's Article 5 collective defence clause.
  • Romania's navy, which patrols for drifting mines and drones, says it does not have enough personnel or equipment for the threat it now faces.

Constanța, Romania — Out on the Black Sea, the Romanian Navy is always on the lookout for the deadly debris of a war it is not fighting. It is a front of the Russia-Ukraine war that most people rarely see, one that runs right up to NATO's doorstep and sometimes crosses into its waters — threatening to pull the alliance, and therefore the United States, into the war, CBS News reported.

Incidents involving drones, mines and commercial ships are surging in the Black Sea, NATO military spokesperson Colonel Martin O'Donnell told CBS News. "In 2025, for example, we saw fewer than 50 incidents in the Black Sea. This year alone, we're talking four to five hundred," he said.

Deadlier than Hormuz for shipping

The roughly tenfold increase threatens a major artery of global grain and fuel shipments. Twenty-five sailors have been killed in the Strait of Hormuz this year, according to the International Maritime Organization, while at least 40 have been killed in the Black Sea in the same period, according to the International Transport Workers' Federation.

"I would say the Black Sea is just as important, and then depending on who you talk to, some might argue could perhaps even be more important … in terms of global trade."

— Colonel Martin O'Donnell, NATO military spokesperson, to CBS News

Any imbalance in the flow of fuel and food "can have global implications that can impact America just as much as it can any of the nations here," O'Donnell said.

A front that keeps spilling over

The maritime front stretches beyond the Black Sea. Over the weekend, Ukraine said it struck an advanced Russian warship and a cargo ship that then drifted, on fire, into the waters of NATO member Finland. On Sunday, Ukraine said it sank a Russian warship docked in Libya.

On land, the spillover is also mounting. On Friday, Poland accused Russia of "intentional provocation" as Russian cruise missiles landed in the country's southeast. Drones have repeatedly entered the airspace of Poland and other NATO countries, mostly near Ukraine but not all, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.

No fence at sea

Three of the six countries bordering the Black Sea are NATO members — Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey. But as Romanian Navy Captain Mihai Iordache explains, defending those borders is nothing like defending them on land. "We do not have a fence into the Black Sea to state this is our border, that is the other border," he said. The Romanian Navy is deploying highly specialized divers and drones, scouring the depths for unexploded weapons.

The Article 5 collective defence clause in NATO's founding charter states that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all 32. Asked whether the alliance will defend itself if necessary, O'Donnell told CBS News: "I would say that there should be no doubt on NATO's willingness and ability to act."

On the Black Sea itself, Captain Iordache warns the Romanian Navy is already stretched thin. "We don't have enough people, personnel, equipment to deal with all the commercial ships and all the drones that we have," he told CBS News during an embed. "Four years ago, we were ready for one drifting mine, and right now we are ready for tens of drifting mines," he said. "Could be hotter, could be colder, who knows. Let's hope for peace."

What to watch

The question hanging over the sea is whether a drone or mine crossing into NATO waters and striking a vessel would provoke a military response from the alliance. NATO has increased surveillance and patrols, but the line between containing the war and becoming part of it now runs through one of the world's busiest grain and fuel corridors — a route whose disruption would be felt in food and fuel prices far beyond the region.
